headline: 12 Million Longleaf Pines Planted Across the Deep South
meta_description: As part of the Million Acre Challenge, 12 million endangered longleaf pine trees have been planted on National Forests to restore wildlife habitat.
summary_short: A major reforestation effort has planted 12 million longleaf pine trees across Mississippi, Georgia, Florida, and South Carolina.
body:
As part of the Million Acre Challenge, 12 million imperiled longleaf pine trees have been planted on National Forests in Mississippi, Georgia, Florida, and South Carolina, restoring critical habitat for wildlife across the region.

The longleaf pine ecosystem was once a dominant feature of the southeastern landscape, providing home to countless species adapted to this unique environment. The species and the animals that depend on it have declined sharply over decades as forests were cleared and fragmented.

This large-scale planting initiative represents a significant conservation commitment to bring these endangered trees back to the four-state region. By restoring longleaf forests on federal lands, the project aims to create healthier ecosystems and secure habitat for the wildlife that has historically relied on these woodlands to survive.
quick_facts: 12 million longleaf pine trees planted across four states
Restoration sites include National Forests in Mississippi, Georgia, Florida, South Carolina
Part of the Million Acre Challenge conservation initiative
Longleaf pines are imperiled species requiring habitat restoration
